topic:
DECIDE PANEL RE-RUN: Agent Role Management ("Agent Studio") — hosted Team/Enterprise scaling. Treat as a strategic differentiator with only one chance to get the foundation right.

PRIOR DECISION ON RECORD (do not re-litigate, build on it): project-docs/decisions/2026-11-09-decide-panel-agent-role-management-agent.md — the panel already approved Agent Studio as foundational, gated on: (1) audited/versioned charter writes with attributable actor, (2) every new role wired into capability_ratings from day one (no hand-authored routing locks), (3) a role deprecation/merge lifecycle including GitHub App identity revocation, (4) a trust/dedup review gate before the upstream GitHub feature-request flow and remote Capability Registry ingestion (Zapier MCP/Composio/Smithery) go live. It also rejected tool-named roles (e.g. "Google Stitch driver agent") in favor of modeling tools as harness_bindings/Capability Registry entries on stable functional roles, and filed synlynk-as-an-MCP-server distribution as a BS-15/gh:#2126 follow-on, not in scope.

SPEC UNDER REVIEW: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-09-vizor-agent-role-management-design.md — 10-role taxonomy (pm/architect/tpm/dev delivery; qa/secops quality-trust; maintainer/infra-devops platform; designer/marketing experience) with per-role mandate/autonomous_authorities/escalation_triggers charters in .synlynk/charters/<role>.json, a Vizor BAU charter editor with Enforced/Guidance-tagged prompt-box fields, a 5-step FTUE role-provisioning wizard, and a Capability Registry (native code hooks / local-harness MCPs+Skills scoped by harness_bindings / remote third-party connector manifests) as one unified manifest shape. Everything so far has been designed assuming a SINGLE local host, single human operator, single state.db, single set of GitHub App identities — no multi-tenant, multi-org, or hosted-service concept exists yet anywhere in the charter schema, Capability Registry, or Vizor UI.

STRATEGIC CONTEXT (from the 2026-11-08 consolidated roadmap, project-docs/2026-11-08-authoritative-roadmap-and-capabilities-reconciliation.md, ratified via decide panel dec-71b3e9a5): synlynk's platform horizon is Horizon 3 / v1.0.0 — "Launch synlynk.com platform services, hosted relay, and public capability benchmarks," including a dynamic shell, user accounts, and workspace registry (spec dated 2026-10-23), an opt-in telemetry pipeline, a public capability index, and ephemeral cloud swarm runners on AWS Spot Docker. Separately, standing project memory (vizor-strategic-position) establishes Vizor's committed tier progression: Local (today, synlynk viz on localhost) -> Team (Vizor synced to synlynk.com workspace via a NATS gate/sync mechanism, post-v1.0) -> Enterprise (org-level Vizor with cross-team visibility, v1.2+). Vizor is explicitly the only web HUD at every tier — there is no separate enterprise admin console planned. synlynk is Apache-2.0 and currently host-local only; no LDAP/SSO/SCIM, no multi-tenant identity model, no network egress policy layer, and no infra-provider abstraction exist anywhere in the codebase today.

Evaluate and give a clear, concrete recommendation on EACH of the following, in order. This is being asked explicitly because the user considers Agent Studio a strategic differentiator with only one real opportunity to lay the foundation correctly — so flag anything in the CURRENT spec's data model (charter schema, Capability Registry manifest shape, GitHub-App-per-role identity model, audit-log design from gate #1 above) that would have to be reshaped (vs. additively extended) to reach Team/Enterprise, and say so explicitly per item, not just abstractly.

1. How does the current spec (single-host charter/role model) scale to the hosted Team/Enterprise platform described in the roadmap and the Vizor tier-progression memory? Where does today's design already generalize cleanly (additive), and where would it have to be reshaped (breaking) once a role/charter can belong to a workspace inside a multi-tenant synlynk.com, not just a single local repo?

2. What specifically should be introduced NOW — in this spec, before Phase 1 implementation starts — purely to avoid a breaking migration later, even though the hosted Team/Enterprise service itself is post-v1.0 and out of near-term scope? Be concrete: e.g. does the charter schema need a workspace/tenant_id field today even if it's always a single local value for now; does the GitHub-App-per-role identity model need an abstraction layer before a hosted identity provider can sit behind it; does the audit log (gate #1) need a schema that's already tenant-scoped.

3. Do we need to provision anything now for LDAP/Active Directory, SSO/SAML, SCIM provisioning, and SOC2 or equivalent enterprise security/compliance posture (audit trail immutability, access reviews, data residency)? Distinguish what must be designed into the data model NOW (even if unimplemented) from what can be built later without reshaping existing structures.

4. How should Agent Studio allow third-party tools to enforce their OWN DLP (data-loss-prevention) / endpoint-based secops policy — given the spec already gives secops "its own policy and tools" and cross-cutting veto authority, and the Capability Registry already has a remote-connector/MCP ingestion path? Is DLP policy itself a Capability Registry entry type, a property on secops's charter, or does it need its own policy-enforcement-point concept distinct from both?

5. How should synlynk support creating infrastructure policy at stack/workspace/global levels — preferred cloud providers, VPC/network configuration, IAM/identity configuration — especially once Horizon 3's cloud swarm runners (ephemeral AWS Spot Docker) exist? Does this belong inside Agent Studio's charter/role model (e.g. as an infra/devops role's "policy" object), or is it a separate policy layer that Agent Studio charters merely reference? Give a clear position.

Then give an overall verdict: does anything in the CURRENT spec (as committed) need to change before Phase 1 starts, specifically to avoid a breaking migration when Team/Enterprise work begins — or is the existing design already forward-compatible as long as the concrete Phase-1 additions from item 2 are made? List concrete action items, each tagged [must-do-now] or [design-now-build-later] or [defer-safely].

300-550 words total, structured by numbered item plus the overall verdict.

inputs.claude:
[model=default; version=2.1.319 (Claude Code)]

1. **Scaling path**: Charter schema and role taxonomy generalize additively — mandate/authorities/escalation_triggers are tenant-agnostic concepts. What breaks: GitHub-App-per-role identity (currently 1 App = 1 role = 1 local repo; a hosted workspace needs 1 role × N member identities × N orgs — reshape, not extension), the Capability Registry's implicit single-filesystem `harness_bindings` (local MCP paths don't resolve across tenants), and the audit log if it's keyed only by actor+timestamp with no workspace dimension — queries become unscopeable later, forcing a backfill migration.

2. **Do now**: Add `workspace_id` (default `"local"`) to the charter JSON schema, Capability Registry manifest, and audit log schema — zero behavioral change today, avoids a mandatory data migration later. Introduce an `identity_binding` abstraction (currently just "GitHub App") so a hosted IdP can be a second binding type without touching the role model. Keep Capability Registry manifests tenant-scoped by convention (`workspace_id` + `harness_bindings`) even though there's only one workspace now.

3. **LDAP/SSO/SCIM/SOC2**: Don't build any of it now — but design the identity_binding abstraction (item 2) so SSO/SCIM slot in as new binding types later without schema change. Audit log should be append-only/immutable in storage semantics now (even SQLite WAL + no UPDATE/DELETE on audit rows) — that's cheap today and is the actual SOC2 prerequisite; retrofitting immutability onto a mutable table later is painful. Everything else (access reviews, data residency) is safely deferred.

4. **DLP/secops**: Model DLP as its own **policy-enforcement-point concept**, not a Capability Registry entry or charter property. Capability Registry entries are capabilities (what an agent *can* call); DLP is a cross-cutting constraint on *data flow* regardless of capability. Secops's charter should *reference* a DLP policy object (by id), same pattern item 5 recommends for infra — this keeps the precedent consistent: charters reference policy, they don't embed it.

5. **Infra policy**: Separate policy layer (stack/workspace/global), referenced by the infra/devops role's charter, not embedded in it — identical reasoning to DLP. This also anticipates Horizon 3 cloud-runner policy cleanly.

**Verdict**: Spec is forward-compatible for Phase 1 **only if** the three additive fields/abstractions in item 2 land now — identity_binding abstraction and workspace_id are the load-bearing ones; skipping them risks the one breaking migration the user wants to avoid. Action items: `workspace_id` field on charter/registry/audit schemas [must-do-now]; identity_binding abstraction layer replacing hardcoded GitHub-App assumption [must-do-now]; append-only audit storage semantics [must-do-now]; DLP-as-policy-reference pattern on secops charter [design-now-build-later]; infra policy object referenced by infra role charter [design-now-build-later]; SSO/SCIM/LDAP connectors, data residency, access-review tooling [defer-safely].

[model=default; version=1.5.3]

**Status:**
1. Last completed task: `54490f92` — Fold decide-panel governance gates into agent role management spec.
2. Next task: Decide panel re-run: Agent Role Management ("Agent Studio") hosted Team/Enterprise scaling review.

---

### 1. Scaling to Hosted Team/Enterprise: Additive vs. Reshaping
* **Generalizes cleanly (additive):** The 10-role functional taxonomy, prompt-box Enforced/Guidance dual-binding model, and Capability Registry manifest shape (`capability_id`, `source`, `scope`, `harness_compat`) remain unchanged across deployment tiers.
* **Requires reshaping (breaking if unaddressed):**
  1. *Flat file storage*: `.synlynk/charters/<role>.json` assumes a single local repository filesystem.
  2. *Single-provider identity*: Hardcoding roles to local GitHub App credentials prevents multi-org and enterprise IAM federation.
  3. *Unscoped audit records*: Storing audit diffs without tenancy boundaries prevents multi-tenant ingestion into hosted Vizor.

### 2. Concrete Introductions Needed NOW (Phase 1)
* **Metadata Envelope**: Add optional, defaulted fields to `charter_schema.py`: `tenant_id: "local"`, `workspace_id: "default"`, and `schema_version: "2.0"`.
* **Polymorphic Identity Binding**: Encapsulate role identity into an abstraction layer: `identity_binding: { "provider": "github_app" | "oidc_workload" | "saml", "subject": "..." }`.
* **Partitioned Audit Log**: Audit events in `state.db` must explicitly include `workspace_id`, `actor_type` (`human` | `agent`), `actor_id`, and `parent_hash` (enabling cryptographic chaining).

### 3. Enterprise Auth, SCIM, and SOC2 Compliance
* **Data model NOW:** Include SOC2 compliance fields in charter metadata: `last_reviewed_at`, `reviewed_by`, and `data_residency_tag` (`global` | `us-only` | `eu-only`). Ensure audit entries include hash-chaining pointers for immutable auditability.
* **Build later (additive):** SAML/SSO assertion handling, SCIM role sync endpoints, and customer-managed encryption key (CMEK) orchestration.

### 4. DLP and Third-Party SecOps Policy Enforcement
DLP is neither an execution tool in the Capability Registry nor prompt guidance in a charter. It must be modeled as a distinct **Policy Enforcement Point (PEP)** middleware filter on the execution/dispatch pipeline. The `secops` role owns the ruleset configuration for this PEP, and all remote MCP/connector traffic must pass through it prior to egress.

### 5. Multi-Level Infrastructure Policy
Infrastructure configuration (VPC, cloud providers, Spot Docker runners) does **not** belong inside Agent Studio charters. It belongs to a separate hierarchical policy layer (`.synlynk/infra.json` or hosted workspace settings). The `infra/devops` role's charter simply references these policies as operational boundaries.

---

### Overall Verdict & Action Items

The current spec is strategically solid, but its underlying data model requires three foundational envelopes before Phase 1 build to avoid breaking migrations when scaling to Team/Enterprise:

* `[must-do-now]` Add `schema_version`, `tenant_id`, and `workspace_id` to the charter schema and audit log.
* `[must-do-now]` Abstract role authentication from raw GitHub App IDs into a polymorphic `identity_binding` schema.
* `[must-do-now]` Add `last_reviewed_at` compliance tracking and cryptographic hash-chaining to the audit schema.
* `[design-now-build-later]` Specify the dispatcher-level DLP/Egress PEP pipeline interface for `secops`.
* `[design-now-build-later]` Define the external `.synlynk/infra.json` schema decoupled from role charters.
* `[defer-safely]` SCIM directory sync, enterprise SSO/SAML brokers, and cloud swarm runner orchestration.

**Position:** Approve the design for Phase 1 implementation subject to incorporating the three `[must-do-now]` schema envelopes into the spec. Agent Studio can then ship locally today with zero technical debt when synlynk.com Team and Enterprise tiers launch.
inputs.codex:
[model=default; version=codex-cli 0.163.0]

1. **Scaling:** The functional taxonomy, Enforced/Guidance distinction, `harness_bindings`, capability ratings, and lifecycle concept generalize additively. However, the current model is not hosted-ready. Charters keyed only by local role/file, registry manifests without ownership or visibility scope, GitHub-App-per-role identities, and a local audit log all assume one trust domain. These must be reshaped around workspace-scoped resources, stable role IDs, versioned revisions, and tenant-aware authorization before Team/Enterprise.

2. **Introduce now:** Add `workspace_id`/tenant scope to charter, capability, identity-binding, and audit records, using an explicit local-workspace value today. Replace role-name identity assumptions with an `identity_binding` abstraction whose backend may currently be GitHub App but later be hosted credentials, organization identity, or delegated user identity. Give manifests issuer, owner, scope, version, provenance, revocation, and allowed egress fields. Make audit events append-only, attributable to a principal (human, agent, service, or integration), with before/after hashes and workspace scope. These are migration-preventing changes, not optional polish.

3. **Enterprise identity/compliance:** Do not implement LDAP, AD, SAML, SCIM, SOC2 controls, or residency now. Do design resource ownership, memberships, roles, policy bindings, data classification, retention, immutable audit-event semantics, exportability, and authorization boundaries now. SSO/SCIM can be added later behind those abstractions; retrofitting tenant-scoped access or immutable provenance cannot safely be additive.

4. **DLP/secops:** DLP is neither merely a Capability Registry entry nor just secops charter text. The registry may describe scanners/connectors, while secops may own policy and veto authority, but enforcement needs a distinct policy-enforcement-point (PEP) concept: evaluated at dispatch, connector invocation, data ingress/egress, and runner endpoint. Policies should support deny/allow, obligations, data classes, destinations, evidence, and third-party endpoint attestation.

5. **Infrastructure policy:** Keep stack/workspace/global cloud, VPC, IAM, residency, and runner policies in a separate policy layer. Agent Studio charters should reference permitted policy scopes and authorize infra/devops actions; they should not contain infrastructure configuration. This separation is essential for ephemeral AWS runners and future provider abstraction.

**Overall verdict:** The committed spec needs foundation changes before Phase 1: [must-do-now] tenant/workspace-scoped IDs, identity-binding abstraction, manifest provenance/scope/revocation, immutable actor-attributed audit events, and a separate PEP/policy reference model; [design-now-build-later] enterprise federation, SCIM, residency, compliance evidence, and cloud-provider adapters; [defer-safely] actual hosted service, LDAP/SAML/SCIM implementation, and remote connector rollout until trust/egress review exists. Without these schema boundaries, Team/Enterprise would require a breaking migration.

synthesis:
Decision: Approve the spec for Phase 1 implementation, conditioned on landing a small, bounded set of additive schema changes before any charter/registry/audit code ships — not as new functionality, but as reshaping-prevention. The three sub-agents converge almost exactly (workspace/tenant scoping, identity abstraction, immutable/attributable audit), and Codex's addition of manifest provenance/revocation fields is a natural extension of the same principle, so I'm folding all four into one punch list.

**[must-do-now]** — schema-only, zero behavioral change today, but each one is genuinely hard to retrofit without a data migration:
1. Add `workspace_id` (default `"local"`) to the charter schema, Capability Registry manifest, and audit log rows. This is the one change every sub-agent independently flagged — unscoped records today become unscopeable (not just hard-to-query) once hosted Vizor needs to filter by tenant.
2. Replace the implicit "role = GitHub App" assumption with an `identity_binding` object (`{provider: "github_app" | ..., subject: ...}`). GitHub-App-per-role is the single most load-bearing thing in the current design that is structurally local-host-only; everything else in the taxonomy survives hosting unchanged, this doesn't.
3. Make audit log storage append-only/immutable in actual semantics (no UPDATE/DELETE path on audit rows, actor attribution required on every row — human/agent/service distinguishable). This is the cheap-now, expensive-later item: SOC2-grade immutability bolted onto a mutable table after the fact is a real migration; designing it in now costs nothing.
4. Add minimal provenance/scope fields to Capability Registry manifests (`owner`, `scope`, `version`) so remote connector ingestion (already planned per the prior decision's gate #4) doesn't have to retrofit identity onto entries that shipped without it.

**[design-now-build-later]**: DLP and infra policy both get the same treatment — neither lives inside a charter or inside the Capability Registry as an entry type. Both are policy-enforcement-point concepts that charters *reference* (secops references a DLP policy id; infra/devops references an infra policy id). Spec the reference shape now; don't build the PEP pipeline or the infra policy schema yet.

**[defer-safely]**: SSO/SAML/SCIM/LDAP implementations, data-residency enforcement, access-review tooling, cloud-provider adapters, and the hosted service itself — all genuinely additive once the `identity_binding` and `workspace_id` seams exist, so no foundation work needed beyond those seams.

Net effect: the committed spec does not need to be re-architected, but it should not go into Phase 1 as-is either — items 1–4 go into the spec as an amendment before implementation starts, everything else stays out of scope exactly as the prior decision already drew the line.

The three sub-agents converge almost exactly (workspace/tenant scoping, identity abstraction, immutable/attributable audit), and Codex's addition of manifest provenance/revocation fields is a natural extension of the same principle, so I'm folding all four into one punch list.
